assumptions: That the alert itself was genuine — it was never corroborated against service data, so a false or misfiring alert has not been ruled out.
That the empty metrics response indicates a read/retrieval failure rather than a real gap in the service's emitted data; neither was confirmed.
That the incident's recorded end time reflects the handoff to escalation rather than the service recovering; no recovery was observed or verified.
That the impact window, if any, is unknown — no customer-facing impact was confirmed or excluded.
No logs were read and no remediation actions were attempted, so no conclusions here rest on service behaviour observed during the incident.
input.executive_summary: An automated monitoring alert reported an elevated error rate on one backend service shortly after midnight UTC on 14 September 2026. The automated responder picked the alert up within a second and tried to pull the service's recent performance data to work out what was wrong, but no data came back at all. With nothing to investigate, the responder handed the incident to a human on-call engineer about one second after the alert arrived. No remediation was performed and no configuration was changed. The timestamps on this incident cover only the automated triage step; they are not a measure of how long the service was degraded, and because the underlying data was unreadable we cannot say from this record whether customers were affected, how many, or for how long. That remains open for the escalated investigation.
input.root_cause: Unknown. The alert fired and the automated investigator immediately queried per-minute metrics for io-shop anchored at 00:15, but the query returned zero minutes of data, so no hypothesis could be formed or tested and the incident was escalated for human diagnosis. The only established fact is a secondary failure — the metrics for the incident window could not be read — which itself has not been diagnosed (it may be a metrics-pipeline or query failure, or genuine absence of data).
